    Topic 6: Conditions and pattern basics

    By the end, you will be able to

    • Use Boolean conditions and if expressions.
    • Match simple patterns and a wildcard.
    • Explain exhaustive matches.

    Prerequisite: Topic 5: Functions, statements, and expressions.

    Choose a branch

    Boolean conditions

    if needs a Boolean condition. Use these operators to compare values and combine conditions:

    • == — equality: count == 0 checks whether count equals zero.
    • > — greater than: count > 0 checks whether count is above zero.
    • < — less than: count < 10 checks whether count is below ten.
    • && — Boolean AND: count > 0 && count < 10 requires both conditions to be true.
    • || — Boolean OR: count == 0 || count == 1 requires at least one condition to be true.
    • ! — Boolean NOT: !enabled reverses the Boolean value of enabled.

    if expressions

    An if can produce a value:

    let label = if count == 0 {
    "empty"
} else {
    "nonempty"
};

    Its branches must have compatible types. Unlike some languages, Rust does not treat integers as truth values: if count is invalid.

    match patterns

    match chooses a branch by pattern and must cover all possible inputs. In this example, the patterns 0 and 1 match those exact counts. &'static str here means a reference to a string literal valid for the whole program; detailed lifetime syntax comes later.

    fn size_label(count: usize) -> &'static str {
    match count {
        0 => "empty",
        1 => "single",
        _ => "multiple", // Wildcard covers every remaining value.
    }
}

    Read the symbols in this function as follows:

    • -> — return-type marker: -> &'static str declares the function's return type.
    • => — match-arm separator: 0 => "empty" connects a pattern to the expression evaluated when it matches.
    • _ — wildcard pattern: _ => "multiple" handles any count not matched by an earlier arm.

    Wildcards and exhaustive matches

    The _ wildcard pattern matches any value not handled by an earlier arm. It covers counts 2 and above here, making the match exhaustive: every possible input has a branch. Without it, the compiler rejects this match because 0 and 1 alone do not cover every usize value.

    Checkpoint 4

    What does the wildcard _ do in size_label?




    Which condition is valid when count is an integer?




    Runnable example

    fn size_label(count: usize) -> &'static str {
    match count {
        0 => "empty",
        1 => "single",
        _ => "multiple",
    }
}

fn main() {
    let count = 3;
    let label = if count == 0 { "empty" } else { "nonempty" };
    assert_eq!(label, "nonempty");
    assert_eq!(size_label(0), "empty");
    assert_eq!(size_label(1), "single");
    assert_eq!(size_label(3), "multiple");
    println!("if: {label}, match: {}", size_label(count));
}

    Run from the repository root:

    rustc examples/01-fundamentals/06-conditions-and-patterns/main.rs -o /tmp/rust-fundamentals-6
/tmp/rust-fundamentals-6

    Expected output:

    if: nonempty, match: multiple

    Exercise

    Add a 2 => "pair" arm before the wildcard, and test 0, 1, 2, and 3. Remove the wildcard temporarily, read the exhaustiveness error, then restore it. Rewrite the empty/nonempty decision as a small function.
